The 1895 print (v2-n368 right-2, line-box lines 23 to 24, y1825 to y1849) sets "Specifically: (a) (Bot.) The trunk, stem, or stalk of a plant. (b) (Zoöl.) The stem …", the italic letter (a) introducing the first of ten parallel subsenses (a) to (j). The record wraps (b) to (j) in sd elements, which the parser makes subsenses 3-b to 3-j, but leaves "(a) " as bare text after "Specifically: " (GCIDE has the same bare "(a)"), so the (Bot.) sense is part of sense 3's own content, has no id 3-a, and renders run into sense 3's definition while (b) to (j) render as subsense blocks. The witnessed ownership is a subsense (a) under sense 3, with "Specifically:" kept on sense 3.

The print reads "Seven wonders of the world. See under WONDERS." (v2-n366 left-2, line-box line 9 y2105, seven-wonders-4x.png). The compound it points to is "Seven wonders of the world" in Wonder's homograph 1 (noun), id seven_wonders_of_the_world, defined "See in the Dictionary of Noted Names in Fiction.". The link resolves to the separate Wonders record, whose only homograph is the adverb "See Wondrous.", so the reader lands on an entry without the compound. The bare-"See under" rule looks for the compound in the link's own target (Wonders) and finds none. A data-target cannot help, because it selects an id inside the target entry the link text resolves to. Resolved by 203e9db: the reference carries data-entry="Wonder" and data-target="seven_wonders_of_the_world".

Each reference glosses Sew as the stitching verb: Cosier "See Sew to stitch", Seam "See Sew to fasten with thread", Suture "See Sew to unite with thread". That is Sew's homograph 3 (transitive verb, "To unite or fasten together by stitches"), id 3, the third printed homograph on v2-n366 right column. The links open the entry top, homograph 1, the obsolete noun "Juice; gravy". Sow's intransitive "To sew. See Sew." gives no gloss, so its target (homograph 3 or the intransitive homograph 4) is not settled and it is listed for information only. These references were not read in print here; their pages are outside this packet. Cosier and Suture now open Sew#3 (08e4232); Seam waits for z30, whose range it may fall in.

The print (v2-n364 right-2, line-box line 192 y1271; set-vt-set-up-a-4x.png) sets "— To set up. (a) To erect; to raise; …" with (a) in the same italic sense-letter form as (b) to (j). The definition "To erect; to raise; to elevate; as, to set up a building, …" is sense (a) of the compound, id to_set_up-a. GCIDE carries the same tagging error (<fld>(a)</fld>).

The print sets "Specifically: —" after sense 4's definition (v2-n364 middle-1, line-box line 28 y247; set-vt-specifically-5x.png), as it does after sense 5. Raw keeps the dash as a dash-only text node between and
; the frozen parser drops that node, so the rendered sense 4 reads "Specifically:" (capture 2368-Set-00.png) while sense 5, whose dash shares a text node with "Specifically:", keeps it.

The print (v2-n365 middle column, "Sett (sĕt), n. See SET, n., 2 (e) and 3.", seen on the whole-page identity read) names Set's noun sense 2 (e), the pile-driving piece "[Often incorrectly written sett.]", whose id is 4-2-e. The resolver reads the number 2 but not the lettered (e), because the record wraps it in an sd element, so the link opens sense 2 rather than 2 (e). Resolved by 08e4232: the reference carries data-target="4-2-e" and opens Set#4-2-e.

The 1895 print (v2-n361 right-1, line-box lines 25 to 28, y918 to y1020) numbers the Math. sense 3, directly after sense 2 and its note, and sets no Engler sense; Gutenberg's main text also numbers it 3, and its 1913-supplement block numbers Bot., Elec. and Com. 1 to 3 separately. GCIDE tags the Bot. paragraph "Webster 1913 Suppl." and inserted it before the printed sense. Under "Later senses after printed ones" (reports/dictionary-audit-decisions.md: "When the print divides or numbers senses differently, the record follows the print. A sense that only GCIDE has follows the printed senses and takes the next number"), Math. is sense 3, the Engler sense follows as 4, and Elec. 5 and Com. 6 keep their numbers.

The 1895 print (v2-n359 right column y1615, right-2 piece: "Sep-tic′i-ty (sĕp-tĭs′ĭ-ty̆), n. [See SEPTIC.] Tendency to putrefaction; septic quality.") refers to the putrefaction adjective Septic, printed at y1164 as the braced pair "Sep′tic, Sep′tic-al, a. … Having power to promote putrefaction.", whose record is the key Septical. The link resolves to the canonical slug septic, the Septic record, whose top homograph is the separate Math. adjective "Of the seventh degree or order" (printed at y1088); its homograph 2 is the separate noun "A substance that promotes putrefaction" (printed at y1241). The alias "Septic" is claimed by both records, and the key Septic wins it, so no data-target on the reference can reach the Septical record: a data-target names an id inside the record the slug opens. Resolved by 1937e18 and 08e4232: the reference carries data-entry="Septical" and opens the Septical record.

Sumpter's "Cf. Seam a weight" glosses Seam as the measure, which is Seam's homograph 5 (noun, "A denomination of weight or measure", printed fifth on v2-n344 right column, y2400), id 5; Sumpter's own etymology names the same LL. sagma/sauma. The link opens the entry top, homograph 1, the noun "Grease; tallow; lard." Seamstress's "See Seam." gives no gloss; the sewing seam (homograph 2, id 2) is the likely sense, from AS. seámestre, but no printed word settles it, so it is listed for information only. Neither reference was read in print here; their pages are outside this packet. Resolved in z30 by out-of-batch-edits.json (z30-link:Sumpter-seam-target): Sumpter's reference opens Seam#5.

The 1895 print (v2-n341 middle-3, the two lines above Sculptor, y2566 to y2621, "tilis. See SCULP-/TOR.]", seen in the v2-n341-middle-3 column piece) sets the name in small capitals, the print's cross-reference style, as Sculp's "[See SCULPTOR.]" on the same page, which the record writes as
Sculptor

A second print reading should confirm before the markup changes.

The etymology Greek reads ἰσχιαδοκός; LSJ and Sciatic's printed etymology give ἰσχιαδικός. Noted by z31e initial review; Ischiadic's own print (volume 1) not checked.

Six references to School mean its homograph 2, the noun from L. schola, Gr. σχολή (Scholar, Scholastic, Scholical, Scholium and Scoley trace that etymon; Scheme's etymology lists it beside Epoch and Hectic), but each opened homograph 1, the shoal noun. The print numbers none of them. Resolved in z31 by supplemental-edits.json (Scholastic, Scholical, Scholium), out-of-batch-edits.json (Scholar, Scoley) and z32's supplemental row for Scheme: each link carries data-target="2".

The 1913 sentence "See Schizophyta, in the Supplement." links to /entry/schizophyta, and no record or alias holds Schizophyta. GCIDE names it only inside Schizomycetes, and the Gutenberg 1913 supplement has no Schizophyta entry. The 1895 print does not set the sentence. The target needs a 1913 supplement witness.

Heretic's "Syn. — Heretic, Schismatic, Sectarian." names nouns, and its usage note defines "A schismatic is one who creates a schism", Schismatic's homograph 2 (noun, printed second on v2-n333). Scarus's etymology "[L. See Scar a kind of fish.]" (v2-n331 middle column) means Scar homograph 5, the fish noun from L. scarus; the link opened homograph 1, "A mark in the skin". Resolved in z32 by out-of-batch-edits.json (z32-link:Scarus-scar-target): the link carries data-target="5".

Fifteen records wrote the genitive of σάρξ as σάρκος (accent on the alpha), from GCIDE and Gutenberg's "sa`rkos". The 1895 print and LSJ (σάρξ, gen. σαρκός) give σαρκός. Sanders is red sandalwood, so its "[See Sandal.]" means Sandal homograph 2, the sandalwood noun; the link opened homograph 1 ("Same as Sendal"). Resolved in z34 by out-of-batch-edits.json (z34-link:Sanders-sandal-target): the link carries data-target="2".
